title: Richmond's streetcar system at its height, 1925
method: Today's buildings are dated by OSM start_date or the City of Richmond's recorded year built; buildings since lost downtown come from the 1924–25 Sanborn tracing. The car lines are placed on today's OpenStreetMap streets, following Harland Bartholomew & Associates' plate 'Early Transit Routes, 1888 & 1925' (City Planning Commission, 1943). Curated outlines are placed from today's street intersections and published descriptions; they are not surveyed. Era rules match OSM names, refs and tags; the first match wins.
about: Richmond opened the first practical electric streetcar system in 1888; by the 1920s it reached the suburbs it had created, from Westhampton to Fulton and from Lakeside to Forest Hill Park.

epochs.title: The streetcar city
epochs.note: Car lines as Harland Bartholomew & Associates mapped them for 1925: within the city limits of the day, with the Lakeside and Westhampton lines running on beyond.

features.name: Westhampton line
features.note: West on Floyd Avenue from Robinson Street to the belt line railroad, under it in a tunnel, then a little north to Grove Avenue; out Grove to Three Chopt Road; then on its own right-of-way beside Three Chopt to Towana Road, and on (the line of today's Campus Drive) to Westhampton Park, which became the University of Richmond's campus in 1914. The right-of-way beside Three Chopt is drawn along the road itself.

features.name: Belmont line
features.route: Broad Street – Sheppard Street – Cary Street – Belmont Avenue
features.note: The Broad Street line's extension west from Robinson Street to Sheppard, south to Cary, later carried on eleven blocks to Garrett Street. Which street carried the last stretch is read from the 1925 plate's 'Belmont' label.

features.name: Broad Street line
features.route: Broad Street, Sheppard Street to Church Hill
features.note: Broad Street, the spine of the system, from the Belmont line's turn at Sheppard Street east to Church Hill. The east end is approximate.

features.name: State Fair Grounds spur
features.route: Boulevard north to the Fair Grounds
features.note: The 1925 plate shows a short spur north from Broad Street ending in a loop. It is drawn here up the Boulevard to the State Fair Grounds (1906–1941, on the site of The Diamond); which street the spur took is not certain.

features.name: Main Street line
features.route: Main Street, Robinson Street to Shockoe
features.note: West Main Street, which the line turned into a commercial street through the Fan, east to Shockoe. The west end is approximate.

features.name: Harrison Street line
features.note: A crosstown link on Harrison Street between the Main, Floyd and Broad lines, as the 1925 plate shows it.

features.name: Reservoir (Byrd) Park line
features.note: Down Robinson Street to Reservoir Park (Byrd Park), one of the trolley's favourite destinations, along Lakeview Avenue as the 1925 plate labels it. The far end is approximate.

features.name: Clay Street line
features.note: Sprague's first line of 1888 ran from Church Hill to Clay and Hancock Streets; the 1925 plate still shows Clay Street. The ends are approximate.

features.name: Brookland and Lakeside line
features.route: 1st Street – North Avenue – Brookland Park – Chamberlayne – Laburnum – Hermitage Road
features.note: Over the First Street viaduct (1891) into Barton Heights, then west along Brookland Park Boulevard, north up the median of Chamberlayne Avenue, west on Laburnum and north on Hermitage Road to Lakeside Park and Lewis Ginter's Lakeside Wheel Club. The run beyond Hermitage Road along Lakeside Avenue is approximate.

features.name: Highland Park line
features.route: 5th Street – Northside Viaduct – Highland Park loop
features.note: North on Fifth Street over the Northside Viaduct (1892) to Chestnut Hill and Highland Park, and after 1908 round a loop by Meadowbridge Road, Milton Street and Highland Street (the cross street joining them, Second Avenue here, is approximate). The Hull Street–Highland Park line was Richmond's last: the last car ran on 25 November 1949.

features.name: Marshall Street line (Fulton)
features.route: Marshall Street Viaduct – Church Hill – Fulton
features.note: Across Shockoe Valley on the Marshall Street Viaduct (1911, since demolished: drawn straight) from College Street to 21st Street at Jefferson Park, out Marshall Street, and down to Fulton along Williamsburg Avenue. The route from Marshall Street down to Fulton is approximate.

features.name: Venable Street line
features.route: 17th Street – Venable Street – 25th Street – Nine Mile Road
features.note: North on 17th Street, east along Venable Street through Union Hill, and up 25th Street to Nine Mile Road, the road the Seven Pines line took out of the city (chartered along 25th to 29th Streets and Nine Mile Road). The federal government bought the Seven Pines line in 1918 for a wartime plant; how far cars ran out Nine Mile Road in 1925 is not certain.

features.name: Jefferson Avenue line
features.note: Up 21st Street and out Jefferson Avenue past Jefferson Park, one of the trolley's pleasure grounds, as the 1925 plate shows it.

features.name: Hull Street line
features.note: Over the Mayo Bridge into Manchester and out Hull Street. Its last car, No. 408 on the Hull Street–Highland Park run, ended Richmond's streetcars on 25 November 1949. The outer end is approximate.

features.name: Forest Hill line
features.route: 7th Street – Free Bridge – Semmes Avenue – Forest Hill Avenue
features.note: South over the river (the free bridge at Ninth Street), down the median of Semmes Avenue through Woodland Heights, and out Forest Hill Avenue to Forest Hill Park and its amusement park, the most popular trolley destination of all. VEPCO proposed taking up the Semmes Avenue tracks in 1933.

features.name: Richmond–Ashland Railway
features.route: Broad and Laurel – Brook Road – Ashland
features.note: The interurban to Ashland, built as the Richmond and Chesapeake Bay Railway (1907) and run as the Richmond–Ashland Railway from 1919 to 1938: from its terminal at Broad and Laurel Streets (814 West Broad), over a half-mile concrete trestle across Bacon's Quarter Branch (drawn straight), then up Brook Road and on to Ashland.

features.name: Virginia State Fair Grounds
features.note: The State Fair grounds on the Boulevard, reached by streetcar, from 1906 until the Army took them over in 1941; The Diamond stands there now. The outline is approximate.

features.name: Fair Grounds racetrack
features.note: The fair's half-mile racetrack, drawn as an approximate oval at the centre of the grounds.

rules.note: Opened 1934 as a toll bridge (rebuilt 1985–88 on much the same line).
Approaches of the 1934 Lee Bridge (approximate: some may be older).
The Huguenot Memorial Bridge, opened 1950 (the low Westham Bridge of 1911 stood just by it).
Opened 1 July 1958; designated I-95 a month later.
Unnamed ramps are dated with I-95.
The 9th Street (Manchester) Bridge was completed in 1973.
A bridge has stood here since John Mayo Jr.'s of 1788; today's dates from 1913.
The floodwall was dedicated on 21 October 1994.
The canal's downtown end, from about 1800 until the railroad took it over (end date approximate); the stretch seen today was re-watered for the Canal Walk in 1999.
David Ross built the mill canal in 1790.
The elevated viaducts and the Triple Crossing were built with Main Street Station, opened 1901.
Railroads reach Richmond from 1836 (the RF&P); lines at grade are dated from then, although today's alignments are later.
Paths are not dated: drawn in today's view only.
Fountains are not dated: drawn in today's view only.
Surface parking: an approximate date, not sourced.
Road bridges not named above (over the rail lines and the interstate) are dated with the viaducts: approximate.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol
dates.note: Completed 1788; the wings of 1904–06 are not drawn apart.
